body: The American Revolution (1775-83), arose from growing tensions between residents of Great Britain’s 13 North American colonies and the colonial government, which represented the British crown.

cards.title: Declaring Independence (1775-76)
body: When the Second Continental Congress convened in Philadelphia, delegates—including new additions Benjamin Franklin and Thomas Jefferson—voted to form a Continental Army, with Washington as its commander in chief.

On June 17, in the Revolution’s first major battle, colonial forces inflicted heavy casualties on the British regiment of General William Howe at Breed’s Hill in Boston. The engagement, known as the Battle of Bunker Hill, ended in British victory, but lent encouragement to the revolutionary cause.

By June 1776, with the Revolutionary War in full swing, a growing majority of the colonists had come to favor independence from Britain. On July 4, the Continental Congress voted to adopt the Declaration of Independence, drafted by a five-man committee including Franklin and John Adams but written mainly by Jefferson.

cards.title: Saratoga: the American revolution Turning Point (1777-78)
body: The British suffered the consequences of this on September 19, when an American force under General Horatio Gates defeated them at Freeman’s Farm in the first Battle of Saratoga.

After suffering another defeat on October 7 at Bemis Heights (the Second Battle of Saratoga), Burgoyne surrendered his remaining forces on October 17. The American victory Saratoga would prove to be a turning point of the American Revolution, as it prompted France (which had been secretly aiding the rebels since 1776) to enter the war openly on the American side, though it would not formally declare war on Great Britain until June 1778. The American Revolution, which had begun as a civil conflict between Britain and its colonies, had become a world war.

cards.title: The End of the Revolution (1781-83)
body: The British removal of their troops from Charleston and Savannah in late 1782 finally pointed to the end of the conflict. British and American negotiators in Paris signed preliminary peace terms in Paris late that November, and on September 3, 1783, Great Britain formally recognized the independence of the United States in the Treaty of Paris.

cards.title: The causes of the revolution
body: The French Society during the Late 18th Century-The French Society comprised it was highly stratified among:
1st Estate: Clergy
2nd Estate: Nobility

3rd Estate: Big businessmen, merchants, court officials, peasants, artisans, landless laborers, servants, etc. Some within the Third Estate were rich and some were poor. The burden of financing activities of the state through taxes was borne by the Third Estate alone.
The Struggle for Survival: Population of France grew and so did the demand for grains. The gap between the rich and poor widened. This led to subsistence crises.

The Growing Middle Class: This estate was educated and believed that no group in society should be privileged by birth. These ideas were put forward by philosophers such as Locke the English philosopher and Rousseau the French philosopher. The American Constitution and its guarantee of individual rights was an important example of political theories of France. These ideas were discussed intensively in salons and coffee houses and spread among people through books and newspapers. These were even read aloud.

cards.title: The Outbreak of the Revolution
body: The French Revolution went through various stages. When Louis XVI became the king of France in 1774, he inherited a treasury which was empty. There was growing discontent within the society of the Old Regime.

In order to solve the economic problems Louis 16th called the meeting of the general estate which had never conduct meeting since 1614. The Estates-General was composed of representatives from then three Estates of French society. The First and Second Estates had about three hundred delegates each. And the third had six hundred delegates.

The meeting of the Estates-General opened at Versailles on May 5, 1789. In the beginning of the meeting members of the Third Estate demanded reform in the voting system of the Estate-General. The king refused to accept their demands.
The Third Estate reacted quickly. On June 17, 1789, it called itself a National Assembly and decided to draft a constitution.

lessons.title: Storming of the Bastille (the immediate cause )

cards.title: Storming of the Bastille (the immediate cause )
body: Louis XVI prepared to use force against the newly formed national assembly. The common people, however, saved the Third Estate from the king’s forces. On July 14, a mob stormed the Bastille, an armory (store for weapons) and prison in Paris, and dismantled it.

A growing hatred of the landholding system, with its fees and obligations, led to popular uprisings. Peasant rebellions took place throughout France and the revolutions spread quickly throughout France in the summer of 1789.

On the night of August 4, 1789, the National Assembly voted to abolish the rights of landlords as well as the financial privileges of the nobles and the clergy. On August 26, 1789 the National Assembly adopted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and the Citizen.
The Declaration was influenced by Enlightenment thought and the American Declaration of Independence and Constitution.

After temporary refusal of the king to accept the national assembly decree and to come to Paris, On October 6(forced by women’s protest in Versailles, the family went to Paris. After their arrival, the king and his family became virtual prisoners in Paris. Later, In June of 1791, Louis XVI and his family tried to escape from France. He was recognized and caught and was forced to return to Paris.

cards.title: Reformation by the National after the revolution in 1791-92
body: The Catholic Church was seen as a part of the old order by the revolutionaries and was forced to reform
National Assembly took over and sold the lands of the Church. The Church was also secularized.
The National Assembly completed a new constitution, the Constitution of 1791, which set up a limited monarchy.

cards.title: War and crisis
body: Many European monarchs fear the revolution would spread so they started to move against the French national assembly. The assembly declared war on Austria in 1792 as response but France was defeated and it became the end of the national assembly as the people demanded more strong and brutal leadership.

In August, radical political groups in Paris, who called themselves a commune (the Paris commune), organized a mob attack on the royal palace and Legislative Assembly. Members of the new Paris Commune imprisoned the king. They forced the Legislative Assembly to suspend the monarchy and call for a National Convention to decide on the nation’s future form of government.
The members of Commune were from the working class, small traders and artisans. With the emergence of the Paris Commune the French Revolution entered a more radical stage.

The commune forced the legislative body to set a national convention to end the era of Monarchy and to establish. Before the convention the commune started to take revenge upon people who resisted the revolution. Members of the Convention split into factions over the fate of the king. Finally, the most radical faction won and it convinced the National Convention to pass a decree condemning Louis XVI to death. On January 21, 1793, the king was beheaded on the guillotine. The execution of the king created new enemies for the revolution, both at home and abroad.
The execution of Louis XVI outraged the kings of most of Europe. An informal coalition of Austria, Prussia, Spain, Portugal, Britain, and the Dutch Republic took up arms against France.

The National Convention gave broad powers to a special committee of 12 people known as the Committee of Public Safety in order to counter these crises. It was dominated at first by Georges Danton and later by Maximillian Robespierre.

The committee of the public safety created a one year of period of terror(1793-94) it used the famous tool to executed any person who goes against the republic it was the Gluten (even the queen herself was a victim of the tool.

The committee ruled for one year and defeated the enemies in and abroad, it refused to stop the terror even after the peace was achieved. At last the terror ended with the death of the architect of the tool Robespierre in 1794.
After the end of terror the legislative body formed a two house of directory called the upper and the lower house.
The era of the directory (1795-1799) was an era of corruption and the economic problems were still unsolved which resulted in coup by the famous general Napoleon Bonaparte in 1799.

cards.title: The rise of Napoleon Bonaparte
body: As a young man Napoleon received a royal scholarship to study at a military school in France. Napoleon’s education in French military schools led to his recruitment in 1785 as a lieutenant in the French army. In 1792, he became a captain. Two years later, at the age of only 24, he was made a brigadier general by the Committee of Public Safety.
In 1796, he was made commander of the French armies in Italy, and he was successful in his campaigns. In 1797, Napoleon returned to France as a hero.
After his defeat in Egypt by British Napoleon returned to Paris and participated in coup of the 1799.
His domestic and foreign policy include:
At home he make peace with Catholic Church and Catholicism became France official religion.
In return, the Pope agreed not to ask for the return of church lands seized in the revolution.

Napoleon’s most famous domestic achievement was his codification of the laws. Before the Revolution, France did not have a single set of laws. Napoleon integrated French laws in seven codes of law. The most important of the codes was the Civil Code or Napoleonic Code. This code preserved most of the ideas of the revolution by recognizing the principle of the equality of all citizens before the law, the right of the individual to choose a profession, religious toleration, and the abolition of serfdom and feudalism. Property rights were also protected.

cards.title: Napoleon’s Empire
body: Napoleon’s huge army defeated the Austrian, Prussian, and Russian armies. Thus, Napoleon got an opportunity to create a new European order. From1807 to 1812, Napoleon became the master of Europe. His Grand Empire was composed of three major parts (the French Empire, dependent states, and allied states).

Napoleon hoped that his Grand Empire would last for centuries however, it collapsed very soon. Two major reasons can explain the fall of Napoleon’s Empire. These were the survival of Great Britain and the force of nationalism.

cards.title: The fall of Napoleon
body: The beginning of Napoleon’s downfall came when he invaded Russia. The Russians had refused to remain his allies.

In June 1812 napoleon grand army marched towards the invasion of Russia. But Russia unlike the expectation of napoleon used retreat and scorched earth policy and suffered the grand army with hunger and thirst when they reach Moscow. At last napoleon was defeated in Russia and his army were forced to retreat in 1813.

The weakened French army. Paris was captured in March 1814. Napoleon was soon sent into exile. The Bourbon monarchy was restored to France and Louis XVIII, brother of the executed king Louis XVI, became the king of France.

cards.title: What Was the Industrial Revolution?
body: The Industrial Revolution was a period of major mechanization and innovation that began in Great Britain during the mid-18th century and early 19th century.
The British Industrial Revolution was dominated by the exploitation of coal and iron.

cards.title: The main points
body: *The first Industrial Revolution began in Great Britain in the 1700s and 1800s and was a time of significant innovation.
*The American Industrial Revolution followed in the late 19th century and was an engine of economic growth in the U.S.
*The Industrial Revolution led to inventions that included the assembly line, telegraph, steam engine, sewing machine, and internal combustion engine.

*Working for businesses during the Industrial Revolution paid better wages than agricultural work. The increase in the number of factories and migration to the cities led to pollution, deplorable working and living conditions, and child labor.

cards.title: How Did the Industrial Revolution Impact Society?
body: Although the Industrial Revolution occurred approximately 200 years ago, it is a period that left a profound impact on how people lived and the way businesses operated.
Arguably, the factory systems developed during the Industrial Revolution are responsible for creating capitalism and the modern cities of today.
Often the wages were low, and conditions were harsh. However, working for such businesses still paid a better living wage than farming.
Production efficiency improved during the Industrial Revolution with inventions such as the steam engine.
The steam engine dramatically reduced the time it took to manufacture products.
Before the use of coal, wood was the primary energy source; coal provided three times more energy than wood, and Britain had large coal deposits.

cards.title: Advantages of Industrialization
body: The Industrial Revolution created an increase in employment opportunities. This led to significant improvements in city planning.
Increased innovation also led to higher levels of education
made life comfortable for many though living conditions for workers remained abhorrent,
This eventually fueled the rise of labor unions that led to improved working conditions and fair wages.

cards.title: Disadvantages of Industrialization
body: It led to a shortage of food production.
An increase in urban pollution.
Working conditions in factories deteriorated. Long hours, inadequate remuneration, and minimal breaks became the norm.
Child labor was a significant issue. Health issues arose for many of the factory workers giving rise to the labor movement throughout the U.S.

cards.title: Rise of socialism
body: In the first half of the 19th century, the difficult conditions created by the Industrial Revolution gave rise to a movement known as Socialism.
Socialism is a system in which society, usually in the form of the state, owns and controls the main means of production, such as factories and utilities.
Early Socialism was largely the idea of intellectuals who believed in the equality of all people and who wanted to replace competition with cooperation in industry.
To later Socialists, especially the followers of Karl Marx, such ideas were impractical dreams. The later Socialists named the earlier theorists utopian socialists.

cards.title: What Key Innovations Took Place During the Industrial Revolution? – Revolutions of 1848
body: Main topics
* Revolutions of 1848: An Overview
* Causes of the Revolutions of 1848
* Impact of the Revolutions of 1848

cards.title: Background – What did Liberal Nationalism represent?
body: ‘Liberalism’ is derived from the Latin word, meaning free. Voting and election rights were granted only to men who owned property.

cards.title: Age of Revolution 1830-1848
body: As conservative regimes tried to consolidate their power, liberalism and nationalism came to be increasingly associated with revolution in many regions of Europe such as the Italian and German states, the provinces of the Ottoman Empire, Ireland and Poland.

The first upheaval took place in France in July 1830. The Bourbon kings who had been restored to power during the conservative reaction after 1815, were now overthrown by liberal revolutionaries who installed a constitutional monarchy with Louis Philippe at its head.

cards.title: A New Conservatism after 1815
body: In 1815, European governments were driven by the spirit of conservation. The Conservatives believed in royalty, Church, civil society, and property and that the family should be preserved.
In 1815, representatives of European countries - Britain, Russia, Prussia, and Austria met in Vienna to form a concert of Europe.

The Bourbon Empire was restored to power, and France lost its lands to Napoleon. The biggest challenge taken by the liberal-nationalists, who criticized the new law-abiding system, was media freedom (free press).

cards.title: Why is 1848 called the year of revolution?
body: 1848 is called the year of revolution because revolutions broke out in multiple European countries this year. Revolutionary turmoil ricked German and Italian states, Italy, Austrian Empire, and Denmark. Most of these revolutions failed at their goal of political liberalization, however.

cards.title: Causes the Revolutions of 1848
body: The Revolutions of 1848 were caused by spread of ideas such as popular sovereignty (arguing for political liberalization of absolute monarchies), nationalism, and socialism. Their more immediate cause was economic crisis in Europe in 1845-48.

cards.title: What did the Revolutions of 1848 mean for France?
body: The revolution of 1848 was initially successful in France, abolishing a corrupt oligarchy of King Louis-Philippe and installing a democratic republic instead. However, the republic survived only two years. In 1850, it was abolished by its democratically elected president, Louis-Napoleon, nephew of Napoleon Bonaparte, who restored the French Empire.

cards.title: Revolutions of 1848: An Overview – Causes of the Revolutions of 1848
body: The revolutions of 1848 in Europe resembled a wave; they started in Sicily in January 1848 and subsequently erupted in other countries.

As mentioned, although particular causes varied across countries, the main revolutions of 1848 causes were the ideas of political liberalization, nationalism, and socialism. These ideas made people demand political change.
The more immediate cause of the revolutions was the economic crisis of 1845-47. Many European countries were struck by poor harvest and famine, making anti-government protests increasingly likely.
Revolutions of 1848: Timeline of Events

The revolutions of 1848 started in January 1848 in Sicily. After the revolution in Sicily achieved a (temporary) success by forcing the King to proclaim a constitution, protests broke out in February 1848 in France and other Italian states, and in March 1848 in the German states, the Austrian (Hapsburg) Empire, and Denmark. There were also minor protests in other countries.

cards.title: Revolutions of 1848: Sicily, Italy
body: Before the outbreak of the revolutions, Italy was divided politically. Its southern part was controlled by the Kingdom of Two Sicilies, a repressive absolute monarchy.

Papal States, governed by the Pope, occupied most of central Italy. Most of the north was controlled by the Austrian Empire, either directly or indirectly, as several smaller Italian states were ruled by branches of the Hapsburg dynasty. The Kingdom of Sardinia-Piedmont occupied the northwestern part of the country and the island of Sardinia.
Due to this political division, Italian revolutionaries had dual goals; political liberalization and Italian unification, the latter resulting from their nationalist views.

These goals were embraced by the King of Piedmont, who proclaimed a liberal constitution and in March 1848, attacked the Austria-controlled Lombardy to aid the anti-Austrian uprisings there. After initial setbacks, Austrians ultimately defeated Italian forces at Novara in March 1849 and restored their rule in Northern Italy. The Pope, who initially supported Italian unification, decided to withdraw his troops, leading to an uprising in Rome and creation of a democratic Roman Republic on February 9, 1849. However, a French military intervention reestablished the Pope's rule on July 3, 1849. The revolution in the Kingdom of Two Sicilies was also crushed by the King in a few months, and absolute monarchy was reintroduced there.

cards.title: The February Revolution – France
body: In contrast to Prussia and Austria, which were absolute monarchies, France, before the February Revolution of 1848, was a constitutional monarchy.

However, the French were growing dissatisfied with the rule of King Louis Philippe I, whose government grew increasingly corrupt, kept suffrage restricted to only 2% of male adults, and repressed the press.

The February Revolution began on February 23, 1848, when protests broke out in Paris following cancellation of a political meeting, leading to the King's abdication in just two days. A republic (known as the Second Republic) was proclaimed.
A workers' uprising that broke out in June 1848 in Paris was brutally crushed by the government.
In December 1848, a charismatic and populist leader, Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte (nephew of Napoleon I) was elected president with 74% of the vote.
He quickly conflicted with the legislature, which did not want to eliminate the constitutional ban on reelection.
In December 1851, Louis-Napoleon unconstitutionally dissolved the legislature, and a year later proclaimed himself the emperor following a rigged referendum.
The February Revolution ultimately resulted in the creation of another authoritarian regime, although of a populist rather than oligarchical character

cards.title: Impact of the Revolutions of 1848
body: In a short term, most Revolutions of 1848 were unsuccessful. In Austria and Italian states, absolute monarchies were introduced after the uprisings were suppressed.
France was a short-term success because it established a democratic republic, but it gave way to an autocracy in just two years.
However, the revolutions noted some success in Prussia and a few other German states, which became more liberal following the events.
Only in Denmark can the 1848 revolution be considered a clear success.

lessons.title: The Unification of Italy and Germany

cards.title: Italy Unified
body: During the middle of the nineteenth century, Italy was divided into seven states, of which only one, Sardinia-Piedmont, was ruled by an Italian princely house. Even the Italian language had not acquired one common form and still had many regional and local variations.
The failure of revolutionary uprisings both in 1831 and 1848 meant that the mantle now fell on Sardinia Piedmont under its ruler King Victor Emmanuel If to unify the Italian states through war.
Through a tactful diplomatic alliance with France engineered by Cavour, Sardinia-Piedmont succeeded in defeating the Austrian forces in 1859.
Apart from regular troops, a large number of armed volunteers under the leadership of Giuseppe Garibaldi joined the fray.

In 1860, they marched into South Italy and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies and succeeded in winning the support of the local peasants in order to drive out the Spanish rulers. In 1861 Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed king of united Italy.

cards.title: Unification of Germany
body: It started with the liberal Nationalist movement of 1848 with the formation of the Frankfurt Parliament but efforts failed.
The move was then taken by Prussia and the responsibility shifted to Prime Minister Otto Von Bismarck.
Bismarck led three wars over a period of seven years with Austria, Denmark and France culminating in a Prussian victory.
Nationalist feelings were widespread among middle-class Germans, who in 1848 tried to unite the different regions of the German confederation into a nation-state governed by an elected parliament.

Prussia took on the leadership of the movement for national unification. its Chief minister, Otto von Bismarck (followed the policy of Blood and Iron), was the architect of the unification carried out with the help of the Prussian army and bureaucracy.
In January 1871, the Prussian king, William I was proclaimed German Emperor in a ceremony held at Versailles.

lessons.title: Europe and North America from 1850 to1914

cards.title: GREAT BRITAIN
body: Great Britain was able to avoid the Revolution in 1848. In the beginning of 19th century, Great Britain was governed by aristocratic landowning classes, which dominated both houses of Parliament.

cards.title: The changes include
body: In 1832, Parliament issued a law that increased the number of male voters.
Another reason for Britain’s stability was its continuing economic growth.
By 1871, Great Britain had a two-party parliamentary system. For the next 50 years, these two parties (the Liberal Party and the Conservative Party) were in and out of power.
By 1900 a new labor party was established
By the end of World War I (1918), all males over age 21 and women over age 30 could vote.

cards.title: France changes include
body: Four years after his election as president in 1848, Louis-Napoleon organized a plebiscite, or popular vote, for the restoration of the monarchy. A substantial majority supported the restoration and on December 2, 1852, Louis-Napoleon became Emperor of France as Napoleon III.
Napoleon III completely controlled the government and limited civil liberties but achieved economic progress

In the 1860s, opposition to some of Napoleon’s economic and governmental policies arose. In response, Napoleon III began to liberalize his regime. Soon after the French defeat in the Franco- Prussian War, however, his empire collapsed.
In 1875, five years after it was proclaimed, the Third Republic gained a republican constitution.

The new government had a president and a legislature made up of two houses. Members of the upper house, called the Senate, were elected indirectly. In the lower house, called the Chamber of Deputies, members were elected by universal male suffrage.

cards.title: The Austrian Empire – Changes include
body: After the Hapsburg rulers crushed the revolutions of 1848 and 1849, they restored centralized, autocratic government to the empire.
But after Austria’s defeat at the hands of the Prussians in 1866. The result was the Compromise of 1867. This Compromise created the dual monarchy of Austria-Hungary.
The two states tied together by a single monarch, and a common army, foreign policy, and system of finances.
Thus, in domestic affairs the Hungarians had become independent.

cards.title: Germany
body: The Constitution of the new imperial Germany begun by Otto von Bismarck in 1871 provided for a two-house legislature. The lower house of the German parliament, the Reichstag, was elected on the basis of universal male suffrage.
By the reign of William II, emperor from 1888 to 1918, Germany had become the strongest military and industrial power in Europe.

cards.title: Russia
body: The Russian czar was still regarded as a divine-right monarch with unlimited power. In 1856, the Russians suffered a humiliating defeat in the Crimean War.
In order to cope with western powers, Czar Alexander II decided to make reforms. Serfdom was the largest problem in Russia.
On March 3, 1861, Alexander issued an Emancipation Proclamation, which freed the serfs. Some conservators did not like the change made. When a group of radicals assassinated Alexander II
In 1881, his son and successor, Alexander III came to power. He abandoned his father’s reform programs and returned to the old methods of repression.

In 1894 Nicholas II began his rule as a czar of Russia. Industrialization began late in Russia but progressed rapidly after 1890. By 1900, Russia had become the fourth largest producer of steel behind.
Growing dissatisfaction and opposition to the czarist regime finally gave rise to the Revolution of 1905.

On January 22, 1905, workers marched to the Winter Palace in St. Petersburg to present a petition of grievances to the czar. Troops opened fire on the peaceful demonstration, killing hundreds. This became known as “Bloody Sunday.” The massacre caused workers throughout Russia to call strikes and led to the Revolution of 1905.

The Revolution was defeated. But Nicholas II was forced to allow civil liberties and create a legislative assembly, called the Duma. These reforms, however, were short-lived. By 1907, the czar had already restricted the power of the Duma, and again used the army and bureaucracy to rule Russia.

lessons.title: Nationalism and Civil War in the United States

cards.title: Nationalism and Civil War in the United States
body: United States national unity was not achieved easily after the adoption of the Constitution. Two factions fought about the division of power in the new government.

The Federalists favored a strong central government. The Republicans, fearing central power, wanted the federal government to be subordinate to the state governments. These early divisions came to an end with the War of 1812 against the British.
By the mid-19th century, the issue of American national unity had reemerged. Slavery had become a threat to that unity.

Although the importation of slaves was banned in 1808, there were four million African American slaves in the South by 1860. The South’s economy was based on growing cotton on plantations, mostly by slave labor.
Thus abolitionism, a movement to end slavery, arose in the North and challenged the slavery in the South.

When the anti-slavery politician, Abraham Lincoln was elected president in November 1860, South Carolina decided to secede from the United States. In February 1861, six more Southern states did the same
And a rival state called the Confederate States of America was formed. In April, fighting erupted between the North and South.

Over 600,000 soldiers died during the war. The Union, with more men and resources, gradually weakened the Confederacy. With the surrender of Confederate forces on April 9, 1865, the unity of the United States was restored.

In 1865, the Thirteenth Amendment to the Constitution was passed. The amendment abolished slavery in the US. The Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments gave citizenship to African Americans and the right to vote to African American males.

By the end of the 19th century, the United States began to expand abroad. The Samoan Islands in the Pacific became the first important United States colony. Hawaii was annexed by the United States in 1898.

In the same year, the United States also defeated Spain in the Spanish-American War. As a result, the United States acquired the formerly Spanish possessions of Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines.

cards.title: CANADA – The Emergence of a Settlers Nation in Canada
body: By the Treaty of Paris in 1763, signed at the end of the Seven Years ’War, Canada passed from the French to the British.
The indigenous people demanded independence However; there were also differences among the colonists.
In 1840, the British Parliament formally joined Upper and Lower Canada into the United Provinces of Canada.
In 1867, however, the British allowed the establishment of a Canadian state (the Dominion of Canada) with its own constitution.
Thus, Canada abolished a parliamentary system and ruled itself, although foreign affairs remained in the hands of the British government.

cards.title: The Working Classes Movement
body: In the 1870s many workers made movements and protests against the industrial governments their main reasons were:
The desire to improve their working and living conditions.
Most of workers blamed the industrialist for the miserable working conditions.

Many workers organization were influenced and motivated by the works of KARL MAARX and FREDRICH ENGLES on the book of communist manifesto written in 1875.both writers favored socialism from industrial capitalism.
Marx believed that all of world history was a history of class struggles. Which encouraged class struggle for class less society led by workers and proletariats.
He also believed that that the final revolution would ultimately produce a classless society. The state (which had been an instrument of the bourgeois interests) would wither away.
Because of the ideas many socialist party grew some of them even overcome the government’s opposition example, the SOCIAL DEMOCRATIC PARTY OF GERMANY ,

In 1889, leaders of the various socialist parties from different countries joined together and formed an association of national socialist groups that would fight against capitalism worldwide. This association was called the Second International. (The First International had failed in 1872.)

cards.title: 3.4.4 International Rivalry
body: Many European nations entered into different alliances such as:
Germany’s chief rival was France. To isolate France, Bismarck made an alliance with Austria-Hungary in 1879. In 1882, Italy joined this alliance (the triple alliance). .

At the same time, Bismarck maintained a separate treaty with Russia and tried to remain on good terms with Great Britain. In 1890 Emperor William 2nd dismissed Bismarck from office for been too diplomatic.
By 1907, an alliance of Great Britain, France, and Russia known as the Triple Entente was formed.
Thus, Europe was divided into two opposing camps. By the beginning of 1914, these camps viewed each other with suspicion. This, among others causes, led to the First World War.

cards.title: Western Society, Culture and Science 1850-1914
body: 3.5.1 Society: different changes occurred in society
The Growth of Cities and the Social Structure.
The improvement of living conditions also enabled cities to grow faster in the second half of the nineteenth century.

By 1900, Europe was divided into two economic zones. Great Britain, Belgium, France, the Netherlands, Germany, the western part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, and northern Italy made up an advanced industrialized areas. The remaining parts of Europe, i.e. Southern Italy, most of Austria-Hungary, Spain, Portugal, the Balkans, and Russia were mostly agricultural. The Movement for Women’s Rights
The massive industrialization of the late 19th century opened the door to new jobs for women.

cards.title: 3.5.2 Science and Scientific Ideas
body: The Scientific Revolution created a rational approach to the study of the natural world. The Industrial Revolution increased interest in scientific research.
The first major change in industry between 1870 and 1914 was the substitution of steel for iron.
In Great Britain, Michael Faraday put together a primitive generator that laid the foundation for the use of electricity.
By 1910, hydroelectric and coal-fired generator enabled homes and factories to be tied to a single, common source of power.
The creation of the light bulb by Thomas Edison in the United States.
A revolution in communications began when Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone in 1876 and Guglielmo Marconi invented the radio in 1901.
In 1903, Orville and Wilbur Wright invented a fixed-wing plane with help of the new engine. In 1919, the first regular passenger air service was established.
In 1859, Charles Darwin published his ground-breaking major work, On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection.
The French scientist, Marie Curie. Discovered that an element called radium gave energy, or radiation, that came from within the atom itself.

cards.title: The cultural developments
body: Many cultural developments also took place such as

Romanticism: The Romantics believed that emotion and sentiment were only understandable to the person experiencing them. Romantics also valued individualism, the belief in the uniqueness of each person.

Realism: The belief that the world should be viewed realistically was closely related to science. Realism, however, also became a movement in the literary and visual arts. The literary Realists of the mid-19th.

Modernism: Between 1870 and 1914, many writers and artists rejected the traditional literary and artistic styles that had dominated European cultural life since the Renaissance. The changes that they produced was called Modernism.

Impressionism was a movement that began in France in the 1870s, when a group of artists rejected the studios where artists had traditionally worked and went out into the countryside to paint nature directly.
One of the most important figures in modern art was Pablo Picasso. He was from Spain but settled in Paris in 1904. He created a new style called Cubism.

cards.title: Colonial rule and Influence in Asia
body: Like Africa, imperialism in Asia dates back to the Age of Exploration. As with Africa, Europeans gained early footholds in Asia in the 1500s and 1600s but the vast Asia empires of the Europeans were not established until the 1700s and 1800s.
First the Portuguese, then the Dutch and finally the French and British established colonies of varying size and consequence in Asia during this period.
While the Portuguese, Dutch, and French established coastal footholds in South Asia, it was the British who ended Mughal rule and brought all of South Asia into their empire.
The colonization of South Asia was carried out by the British East India Company which was motivated by lucrative commodities like cotton, spices, tea, and opium.

cards.title: INDIA
body: The British East India Company (BEIC) used a combination of diplomacy and warfare to gain control of India.

By the mid-1700s the once powerful Mughal Empire had become highly decentralized, the BEIC capitalized on this and offered services including military protection, tax collection, and administration to local rulers in exchange for access to trade.
Over time, the BEIC became the dominate power in the region and political power shifted from the Mughal Emperor and local rulers to the BEIC officers.
To facilitate BEIC administration of such a vast territory, the company employed a multitude of both native administrators and soldiers (called sepoy).
The British gradually took over most of India completely. By 1857 the Indian sepoys triggered the Indian revolt which spread to become the First Indian War of Independence.
Following this war, administrative functions were transferred from the chartered British East India Company to the British government in 1858.
Thus, India came under the direct control of the British crown with the viceroy entrusted with governing the sub-continent.

British rule in India brought hardship to millions of Indians in both the cities and the countryside. When Western education was introduced in India, Indians were influenced by it, but the inequalities between the British ideals of governance and their treatment of Indians became

In response to degrading treatment, some educated Indians decided to establish the Indian National Congress that demanded that Indians be recognized as equals with the British and that they have the right to govern themselves.
The philosophy of “white man’s burden” brought schools, hospitals, and improved food distribution systems.

Trade brought railroads and telegraphs. Highly lucrative commodities like cotton and opium combined with India’s strategic. Location along trade routes to East Asia made India the “crown jewel” of the British Empire for over 90 years.

cards.title: EUROPEAN INFLUNCE IN CHINA
body: The Qing Dynasty of China continued to view their home as the Middle Kingdom surrounded by barbarians with nothing to offer the culturally superior Chinese. This attitude led to the creation of the foreign trade area (CANTON SYSTEM).

The Chinese government limited foreign merchants to a small number of ports, with Canton being the most significant. At these ports, merchants were only allowed to purchase Chinese goods with silver bullion..
To remedy this trade imbalance, the British turned to highly addictive opium, which they began to market for recreational use in Chinese ports.
British marketing efforts were widely successful and before long the trade imbalance was reversed and massive numbers of Chinese were addicted to opium.
The Chinese reacted strongly. They made opium trade illegal and asked the British government to stop the opium traffic.
The British responded with force and started the Opium War (1839–1842). In the war the Chinese were defeated and the Qing dynasty made peace.
The opium war ended with the Nanjing treaty, by this treaty five ports were opened for the western trade and Hong Kong was given to British.

cards.title: The Tai Ping Rebellion
body: In the meantime, the failure of the Chinese government to deal with internal economic problems led to a peasant revolt, known as the Tai Ping Rebellion (1850–1864). The Tai Ping Rebellion found many followers because it called for social reforms. These reforms included giving land to all peasants and treating women as equals of men.

In March 1853, the rebels seized Nanjing, the second largest city of the empire, and massacred 25,000 men, women, and children. The revolt continued for 10 more years but gradually began to collapse. Europeans decided to help Qing dynasty when they realized the destructive nature of the Tai Ping forces. In 1864, Chinese forces, with European aid, recaptured Nanjing and destroyed the remaining rebel force.

cards.title: The Open Door Policy
body: When foreign pressure on the Qing dynasty grew stronger, the United States wanted to secure its trading interest with China. In 1899, the U.S. presented a proposal that ensured equal access to the Chinese market for all nations and preserved the unity of the Chinese Empire. This was called the Open Door Policy.

cards.title: The Boxer Rebellion
body: The Boxers were angry by the foreign occupation of Chinese lands. They also disliked Christian missionaries and Chinese converts to Christianity who seemed to threaten Chinese traditions. At the beginning of 1900, Boxer units were operating in the countryside and killed foreign missionaries and Chinese Christians.

The European powers army restored order and demanded more concessions from the Chinese government. The Chinese government was forced to pay a heavy indemnity to the powers that had crushed the uprising. This further weakened the Chinese government.

cards.title: Causes of the revolution includes
body: The leader of the revolution Sun Yat-sen believed that the Qing dynasty was in a state of collapse and could no longer govern the country.
The Qing dynasty’s failure to improve conditions in China.
Sun believed that China should follow the model of Western countries, he was also convinced that the Chinese people were not ready for democracy.

He instead developed a three-stage reform process that included; (1) a military takeover, (2) a transitional phase in which Sun’s own revolutionary party would prepare the people for democratic rule, and (3) the final stage of a constitutional democracy.
In 1905, Sun united radical groups from across China and formed the Revolutionary Alliance, which ultimately became the Nationalist Party.
Sun’s party was forced to negotiate with General Yuan Shigai, who controlled the army. General Yuan agreed to serve as president of a new Chinese republic and to allow the election of a legislature.
With no popular peasants support to its democratic objectives though the revolution of 1911 was able to end the Qing dynasty, it produced no new political or social order.

cards.title: An Era of Civil War
body: Yuan, as president, ruled in a traditional manner and even tried to set up a new imperial dynasty. And used murder and terror to rule later calming himself president for life.
Yuan’s dictatorship led to clashes with Sun’s party, which was renamed the Kuomintang or Nationalist Party. When Yuan dissolved the nationals party Sun Yat-sen fled to Japan.
Yuan died in 1916. For the next several years, China entered into civil war as the power of the central government disintegrated and military warlords seized power in the provinces.
The coming of Westerners to China affected the Chinese economy in three ways. They
(1) introduced modern means of transportation and communications;
2) created an export market;
(3) Integrated the Chinese market into the 19th-century world economy.
(4) At the same time, however, China was harmed by these developments. Its local industry was mainly destroyed.
(5) In the cities, educated and wealthy people had been influenced by the growing Western culture. Confucian social ideals were declining rapidly.

cards.title: Colonialism and Independence Movements in Latin America
body: After the treaty of Tordesilas both Portugal and Spain tried to consolidate their grasp in Latin America especially in the 16th c Portugal controlled Brazil but Spain created a very vast empire in here.

cards.title: Creation of a new Society
body: In 1501 Spain allowed the intermarriage of natives and Spaniards this created different people like the MESTIZOES (European and Latin American offspring), MULATTOSE, and other African European offspring's.
Economic benefits for the Europeans came from; Mining (gold and silver), creation of immense state by the Europeans in Farming, and trade.
Christianizing the natives was giving to Catholic Church. Besides the Catholic Church built cathedrals, orphanages, schools and hospitals.
The colonialism created new social structure with peninsular (European viceroys) at the top and creoles European and native descendants at the middle and mestizos.
The national movement in L.A started by the middle class, especially after the Napoleonic wars the creoles started organizing revolutions.
On January 1, 1804, the western part of Hispaniola, now called Haiti, announced its freedom and became the first independent state in Latin America.
Beginning in 1810, Mexico too, experienced a revolt. The first leader of Mexican independence movement was a priest called Miguel Hidalgo. In 1821, Mexico declared its independence from Spain.
Starting from 1801-1825 all L.A got freedom led by famous nationalist like Simon Bolivar and Jose de san Martin.

body: Starting trade from 1800s the slave decline and the Europeans changed another form of trade which asked permanent settlements of Europeans in Africa and this started colonialism.
In West Africa British set up colonies in West Africa in gold coast and Sierra-lone in 1874 & A
French also created the largest colonial empire in West Africa the French West Africa in 1900.In 1900 Germany established colony in Togo, Cameroon, Tanzania &Namibia.

cards.title: North Africa -Egypt
body: Mohammed Ali established a separate empire in Egypt in 1805 known as the Mamluk dynasty .He modernized Egypt.
In 1854 the project of opening Suez Canal was started by French engineer Ferdinand de lespese and ended in 1869.
As the gate to three continents Suez Canal became strategically important and Britain bought share in 1875.
The Egyptians revolted in 1881 hating the European dominance, but it was crushed but Britain and Egypt became British protectorate in 1914.
Sudan became independent by the Mahdi revolution led by clerk Mohammed Ahmad in 1881 but British crush the revolution and Sudan became its colony.
Algeria starting from 1872 became French settler colony, soon France made morocco and Tunisia under her protectorate in 1912.
In north east Africa Italy set up colony in Eritrea and Somali but defeated in attempt to control Ethiopia in 1896.

cards.title: Central Africa
body: Central Africa became famous after the coming of the famous explorer David Livingstone in 1800s.

After his death henry Stanly continued his legacy and asked British for help but British refused. King Leopold 2ND of Belgium accepted him and he crated the largest colonial empire in central Africa .soon France also established colony here.

cards.title: East Africa
body: In east Africa British and Germany rivaled for colonies .and agreed by the berlin conference .British took Kenya and Germany Tanzania and Zanzibar, Mozambique to Portugal and Rwanda to Belgium.

The Berlin Conference was conducted between 1884-85 in Germany to stop any conflicts between Europeans in Africa. The were asked just to register their colony between Berlin office to get recognition.

cards.title: South Africa
body: The Boers or Afrikaners were the first white settlers at the tip of South Africa before 1800s.
But after the Napoleonic wars British controlled it and encouraged settlers in what then called cape colony.
The Boers opposed and created their own cities the Transvaal and Orange Free State (South Africa.
In the interior the native blacks were organized under the Zulu under their leader SHAKA ZULU they entered in to several conflicts with the white supremacist the Boers.
Things started to change with coming of the famous successful business man Cecil Rhodes who controlled Rhodesia present day Zambia and Zimbabwe.

Both British and the Boers agreed to solve their differences and create South African under British colony with separated free gov’t led by only whites .in 1910 the south African republic gov’t was created.

cards.title: Introdution
body: World War I (WW I), also known as the Great War, lasted from 28 July 1914 to 11 November 1918.WW I was fought between the Allied Powers and the Central Powers. The main members of the Allied Powers were France, Russia, and Britain. The United States also fought on the side of the Allies after 1917.The main members of the Central Powers were Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, and Bulgaria.

cards.title: Causes of the War
body: There was no single event that led to World War I. The war happened because of several different events that took place in the years building up to 1914.

The new international expansionist policy of Germany: In 1890 the new emperor of Germany, Wilhelm II, began an international policy that sought to turn his country into a world power. Germany was seen as a threat by the other powers and destabilized the international situation.

Mutual Defense Alliances: Countries throughout Europe made mutual defense agreements. These treaties meant that if one country was attacked, allied countries were bound to defend them. The Triple Alliance-1882 linking Germany with Austria-Hungary and Italy. The Triple Entente, which was made up of Britain, France, and Russia, concluded by 1907.Thus, there were two rival groups in Europe.

Imperialism: Before World War I, Africa and parts of Asia were points of contention among the European countries because of their raw materials. The increasing competition and desire for greater empires led to an increase in the confrontation that helped push the world into World War I.

Militarism: As the world entered the 20th century, an arms race had begun. By 1914, Germany had the greatest increase in military buildup. Great Britain and Germany both greatly increased their navies in this time period. This increase in militarism helped push the countries involved into war.

Nationalism: Much of the origin of the war was based on the desire of the Slavic peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina to no longer be part of Austria Hungary but instead be part of Serbia. In this way, nationalism led to the War.

cards.title: The immediate cause
body: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand: In June 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, was shot while he was visiting Sarajevo in Bosnia. He was killed by a Serbian nationalist Gavrilo Principe , who thought that Serbia should control Bosnia instead of Austria. Because its leader had been shot, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia. As a result Russia got involved as it had an alliance with Serbia. Germany then declared war on Russia because Germany had an alliance with Austria-Hungary.

Britain declared war on Germany because of its invasion of neutral Belgium - Britain had agreements to protect both Belgium and France. Some of the major battles during the war included the First Battle of the Marne, Battle of the Somme, Battle of Dannenberg, Battle of Gallipoli, and the Battle of Verdun.

lessons.title: Course of the First World War

cards.title: Course of the First World War
body: The conflict developed on several fronts in Europe, Africa, and Asia. The two main scenarios were the Western front, where the Germans confronted Britain, France and, after 1917, the Americans. The second front was the Eastern front in which the Russians fought against Germans and Austro-Hungarians.

cards.title: The western front
body: The war zone that included Belgium and northern France was called the Western Front. Germany had a plan to invade France through Belgium that’s why it invaded Belgium in august 4 which led to the entry of Great Britain to the war.

Once the Germans failed to reach Paris, the war quickly turned into a stalemate. Both the French and German forces dug hundreds of kilometers of trenches that stretched from the English Channel to the frontiers of Switzerland. These trenches were protected by barbed wire, land mines, and machine guns. They were separated from each other by a strip of territory known as no-man’s land.

The new method of fighting (Trench Warfare or War of Attrition) was new to the 1st world war generals. The no man’s land was unbreakable though they send thousands of soldiers. In 1916, for example, seven hundred thousand soldiers died over a few kilometers of land at Verdun, France.

cards.title: II.The Eastern Front
body: On the Eastern Front, Russia and Serbia fought against Austria-Hungary, Germany, and Turkey. In contrast to the Western Front, the war on the Eastern Front was marked by mobility. The cost in lives, however, was equally enormous.

At the beginning of the First World War, the Russian army moved into eastern Germany. But, it was decisively defeated. On the other hand, Russia and Serbia defeated Austria-Hungary and threw it out of Serbia. To make matters worse, the Italians betrayed their German and Austrian allies and attacked Austria in May 1915.

After it was defeated by Russia and Serbia, Austria-Hungary got help from its ally, Germany. Then the combined forces of Germany and Austria-Hungary defeated the Russian army. Russia suffered a very heavy casualties of 2.5 million killed, captured or wounded. It was almost knocked out of the war. Encouraged by their success, Germany and Austria-Hungary attacked and eliminated Serbia from the war.

cards.title: Widening (Spread) of the War
body: After the stalemate in western front different empires and countries were drawn to the war. Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria joined the central powers in 1915 .On May 1915 Italy turned to the allies. By 1917, the war that started in Europe became a world war. Britain encouraged Ottoman provinces in the Middle East to revolt against the Ottoman Empire. In 1918, British forces destroyed the Ottoman Empire in the Middle East. The Allied powers also took advantage of Germany’s preoccupation in Europe and its lack of naval power to seize German colonies in Africa and elsewhere. Japan, Australia, New Zealand, and China also joined the war on the side of the Allies.

cards.title: The entry of USA
body: At first the United States tried to remain neutral. As World War I continued, however, it became more and more difficult to remain neutral. The immediate cause of the United States entry into the war was a naval conflict between Germany and Great Britain.

In May 1915, a British ship named Lusitania was sunk by a German submarine. As a result, about 1100 civilians, including over 100 Americans, were killed. This greatly angered the United States. After strong opposition from the US, Germany stopped its unrestricted submarine attacks in 1915.

However Germany restarted sinking hundreds of allied ships killing thousands of civilians and On May 1917 USA officially entered in to the war sending one million troops. This greatly shifted the balance of power to the favor of the allies.

cards.title: 7.3 The Russian Revolution
body: The Russian revolution was a clash between the aristocratic monarchy of Tsar Nicholas 2nd and the people of Russia. The people specifically demanded peace and bread (the withdrawal of Russia from WW1 and economic reforms. Several causes led to the revolution of 1917 such as:
Industrially and technologically weak army.
Economic disasters caused by the war.
Tsar Nicholas 2 frequently usage of the army to suppress the people.

cards.title: The Beginning of the Revolution
body: In February 1917, the Russian government started bread rationing in the then capital city of Russia Petrograd (formerly known as St. Petersburg) after the price of bread had risen sharply. However this erupted an uprising in the capital city by thousands of women on 10th March, 1917. As usually Tsar Nicholas 2nd ordered the troops to fire upon the mob but the soldiers refused and sided with the uprising. This eventually ignited the 1917 revolution.

cards.title: The effects of the revolution
body: On 12 March 1917, the Russian legislative body known as Duma established a provisional government headed by Alexander Kerensky.
The provisional government decided to continue Russia’s involvement in the First World War.
The above decision led to protest from different protest groups especially the Soviets (The Soviets were local councils composed of representatives of Russian workers and soldiers).

The rise of the Bolsheviks; ‘Bolsheviks’ meaning majority in Russian, was a small faction of the Russian Marxist party known as the Social Democratic party. It was formed by a Russian Marxist named Vladimir I. Lenin in 1903.

Lenin and his comrades arrived at Petrograd, they began to unite the Soviets. They promised the people the following three things: “Peace, Land, Bread;” “Worker Control of Production;” “All Power to the Soviets.”
In November 6, 1917, the Bolshevik forces seized the Winter Palace (the seat of the provisional government). The provisional government quickly collapsed with little bloodshed.

lessons.title: The result of the October 1917 revolution war

cards.title: The result of the October 1917 revolution war
body: The congress appointed Lenin as head of the new government (communist).
In March 1918, Lenin signed the peace treaty of Brest-Litovsk with Germany and ended Russia’s involvement in the war.
Besides, the Bolshevik government nationalized all land and distributed them to the peasants.
The rise of civil war because of the opposition groups like the royalists, anti-Lenin socialists, and liberals.
The liberals in general known as the white force helped by the allied forces fought against the red army of the Bolsheviks .The red army decisively won in 1920.

lessons.title: The end of the first World War

cards.title: The end of the first World War
body: Finally after the German offensive in the spring of 1918, the Allied counterattack managed to force a decisive retreat of the German army. The defeat of its Germany’s allies and the revolution in Germany that dethroned Wilhelm II (German Emperor), brought about the signing of the armistice on November 11, 1918. The Great War was over.

cards.title: Consequences of the war
body: Economic consequences: World War I cost the participating countries a lot of money. Germany and Great Britain spent about 60% of the money their economy produced. Countries had to raise taxes and borrow money from their citizens. They also printed money in order to buy weapons and other things they needed for war. This led to inflation after the war.

Political Consequences: World War I brought an end to four monarchies: Czar Nicholas II of Russia, Kaiser Wilhelm of Germany, Emperor Charles of Austria and the sultan of the Ottoman Empire had to step down.

New countries were created out of old empires: Austria- Hungary was carved up into a number of independent states. Russia and Germany gave land to Poland. Countries in the Middle East were put under the control of Great Britain and France. What was left of Ottoman Empire became Turkey.

Social Consequences: World war changed society completely. Birth rates declined because millions of young men died (eight million died, millions wounded, maimed (to lose limbs), widows and orphans). Civilians lost their land and fled to other countries.
The role of women also changed. They played a major part in replacing men in factories and offices. Many countries gave women more rights after the war had ended, including the right to vote.
The upper classes lost their leading role in society. Young middle and lower class men and women demanded a say in forming their country after the war.

cards.title: Treaty of Versailles: On June 28, 1919
body: World War I officially ended with the signing of the Treaty of Versailles. The Treaty of Versailles was an attempt to prevent the world from going into another war. It is organized in several chapters each having different clauses.

cards.title: Territorial clauses
body: *France regained Alsace and Lorraine from Germany.
*Eupen and Malmedy passed into the hands of Belgium from Germany.
*Eastern territories were annexed by Poland which caused East Prussia to become territorially isolated.
*Danzig and Memel, former Baltic German cities were declared free cities.
*Denmark annexed northern Schleswig-Holstein.
*Germany lost all of its colonies and the victors annexed them.
Military clauses:
*Drastic limitation of the German navy. Dramatic reduction of the Army (only 100,000 troops, prohibition of having tanks, aircraft and heavy artillery).
*Demilitarization of the Rhineland region.

cards.title: War Reparations
body: The treaty declared Germany and its allies responsible for all 'loss and damage' suffered by the Allies and as a consequence they were forced to pay war reparations to the victors.

cards.title: Other Treaties
body: *The Treaty of Neuilly, signed with Bulgaria. The small Balkan country suffered several territorial losses, in the benefit of Romania, Greece and a brand-new country: Yugoslavia.

*The Treaty of Sevres (1920) signed with Turkey .The Treaty of Sevres was extremely hard and led to the Turkish national rebellion, which was led by Kemal Ataturk. This also led to the war against Greece, which occupied large areas of Anatolia.
*other important social and ideological changes The U.S., which had won the war but had not experienced the conflict on its territory, became a first world power.
The triumph of the Soviet Revolution (Russian Revolution) and the social crisis that followed the war encouraged workers in many countries to protest, creating a pre-revolutionary climate.

The extreme nationalism experienced during the war, coupled with fear of a Communist revolution, encouraged the middle-class populations of some countries to move to the extreme right. This created a hotbed of fascist movements.

Creation of the League of Nations: The League of Nations was an international diplomatic group developed after World War I as a way to solve disputes between countries before they erupted into open warfare. A precursor to the United Nations, the League achieved some victories but had a mixed record of success.

cards.title: Focus question: What does it mean by interwar period?
body: The term “interwar” refers to the period that stretches from the end of the First World War in 1919 to the beginning of the Second World War in 1939.
The interwar period was characterized by difficult economic problems and emergence of dictatorial regimes in Italy, Germany, Russia, and Eastern Europe.
Elsewhere in Africa, the Middle East, Asia and Latin America (South America), the interwar period was characterized by the rise of nationalism and national movements.

cards.title: Efforts for Peace and Security
body: The peace settlement at the end of World War I had sought to bring peace among the warring states. It created the League of Nations to guarantee collective peace and security.

From the beginning, however, the peace settlement left many states unhappy. Eastern Europe was beset by border disputes and many Germans felt bitter about the Treaty of Versailles and vowed to revise it.
Some of the weakness of the league of nations was:
The absence of powerful countries like USA, JAPAN, ITALY and LATER GERMANY also withdraw.
Lack of army made the league unable to implement its decisions.
Some of the events that the league of nations failed to stop include:
Failed to stop border dispute in Eastern Europe.
Failed to stop japan invasion of china territory called Manchuria in 1931.
Failed Germany invasion of Poland and Czechoslovakia in 1939 and 1938 respectively.
Failed to stop Italian invasion of Ethiopia in 1936. And other more.

cards.title: The Question of Reparation
body: Between 1919 and 1924, France demanded a strict enforcement of the Treaty of Versailles. It pressured Germany to pay the reparations agreed in the Treaty. In April 1921, the Allied Reparations Commission decided that Germany pay 132 billion German Marks (33 billion U.S. dollars), payable in annual installment of 2.5million Marks. Germany made its first payment in 1921.

By the following year, however, the German government announced that it was unable to pay any more because of financial problems. France was outraged and sent troops to occupy the Ruhr Valley, Germany’s main industrial and mining center. As a result, German workers went on strike, and their government paid them salaries by printing more paper money. Printing more paper money resulted in higher inflation in Germany.

The economic problems in Germany created unemployment, hyperinflation, loss of life time savings and etc. Strikes by German workers of the Ruhr and British and American protests against the occupation forced France to withdraw from the Ruhr Valley. In August 1924, an international commission produced a new plan for reparations. This new plan was known as the Dawes Plan, after the American banker who chaired the commission. The plan had two objectives:
Reduce the net payment Germany must pay annually based on its ability.
And give 200 million $ for recovery European and Germany economy.
A brief period of European prosperity followed, but it only lasted from 1924 to 1929.

cards.title: The Great Depression
body: A depression is a period of low economic activity and rising unemployment. It was start in 1920s and throughout 1930s,the economies of western countries collapsed. The great depression had big negative consequences on the social, economic, and political conditions of western countries It devastated public morale and led to the rise and strengthening of extreme political parties. The fundamental cause of the depression can be found in the inherent problems of capitalist economic system.
Uneven distribution of land and resource.
Unregulated free market.
The serious decline of economy.

The full United states stock market.1924s the U,S stock market gave to Germany loan under the Dawns plan. Germany needed the US loan to pay reparations to France and Great Britain. In October 1929, the US stock market crushed and the prices of stock collapsed.

In fear US investors withdrew even more money from Germany and other European markets. This withdrew even more money from Germany and other European market. As a result, industrial production declined, and unemployment rose.

cards.title: EFFECTS OF GERAT DEPRESSTION
body: Unemployment: During 1932,the worst year of depression, nearly one British worker in every four hours unemployed. About six million Germans or roughly 40% German labor force were out of work. Millions of Americans were left without adequate food, shelter, and clothing. However few people died from starvation.

Social changes: The economic crises had also affected the roles of men and women. Women able to get low paying jobs as servants, house cleaners and laundresses while many men remained unemployed, either begging on the streets rates or staying at home to do household tasks.

Political changes: the great depression also increased government activity in the economy. Another effect is the renewed interest in communism. Finally, the great depression led many people to join extreme parties such as the Nazis in Germany and the Fascist party in Italy.

lessons.title: Interwar Political Developments in Europe and U.S.A

cards.title: 1. EUROPE
body: In a number of European countries, women were allowed to vote. But countries such as France, Italy, and Switzerland did not allow women to vote. (Women gained the right to vote in1944 in France, in 1945 in Italy, and 1971 in Switzerland.)
In the 1920s, Europe seemed to be returning to normalcy. However, this was not an easy process.

cards.title: I.Germany
body: The Weimar Republic faced many problems from the beginning. One of the problems was the economy.
It pushed many of Germany’s middle class, like teachers and civil servants, toward political parties that were opposed to the Weimar Republic.
As a result of the Great Depression, about four and half million Germans became unemployed in 1930.
The depression created fear and insecurity among Germans and encouraged the rise of extremist parties like the Nazi.

cards.title: II. France
body: After the defeat of Germany in WWI, France became the strongest power in Europe.
However, France, too, suffered financial problems after the war.
France had a relatively stronger economy than other countries; it did not suffer the full impacts of the Great Depression until 1932.
The economic decline then led to political crises in the country. Between 1932 and 1933 only, six governments were formed as the country passed through political chaos.
Finally, in June 1936, a coalition of leftist parties formed a government known as the Popular Front government.
The Popular Front government gave French workers
The right to collective bargaining, i.e., the right of workers’ unions to negotiate with employers over wages and working hours.
In addition, the government fixed working hours to a 40-hour workweek in industry and granted two-week annual paid vacation to workers.

cards.title: III.Great Britain
body: Britain had lost many markets for its industrial products. In many places, the United States and Japan replaced Great Britain as the main exporters of industrial products.
British industries declined and the rate of unemployment increased. In 1921, two million Britons were unemployed.
Moreover, the return of large numbers of soldiers from the war pushed up prices and drove down wages.
As the British economy worsened, the conservative government broke apart. In 1924, the first labor government came to power promising to improve the conditions of British workers.
But, the labor government also failed to fulfill the needs of British workers. Therefore, after only one year in power, the labor government was brought down by a series of workers’ strikes in 1925.

The Labor party was elected in 1929 in coalition with the Liberal party. The coalition tried to introduce a program of social welfare and full employment. But before it started to implement its policies, the Great Depression began.
The depression hit Britain hard. Unemployment rose to 2.5 million within a year and to 3 million by the beginning of 1933. The Labor prime minister was forced to resign in 1931.

The policy of New Deal was aimed at creating recovery and reform. It also included relief for the homeless and destitute.

lessons.title: Cultural Developments of the Interwar Period

cards.title: 1. Mass Culture: Radio and Movies
body: Some of the most important technological innovations that influenced the post First World War cultural developments were the:
Invention of radios and movie cameras.
Radio was invented by an Italian electrical engineer, Guglielmo Marconi, at the end of the 19th century.
On the other hand, movies (motion pictures) emerged in the 1890s. Shortly before WWI, full length movies began to emerge. After the end of WWI, cinema became a popular form of mass entertainment.

cards.title: 2. Mass Leisure in Europe
body: After WWI, the eight-hour workday became the normal practice for many office and factory workers in Europe.
This gave long free hours to many people. As a result, leisure activities; such as sporting events, travels, concerts, operas, and films, became common.
Travelling was made much easier by the production of trains, buses and cars. Thus, travelling became widespread pastime for many Europeans.

One of the most important post WWI writers was James Joyce. Joyce’s most famous book is the Ulysses.
Ulysses tells the story of one day in the life of ordinary people in Dublin by following the flow of their inner thoughts.

cards.title: Background
body: Between 1919 and 1939, national movements emerged in Africa and Asia. These movements sought to free their countries from European colonization.
Though none of the movements were not successful they left a legacy to the post ww2nd nationalist movement.

lessons.title: NATIONALISTS AND NATIONAL MOVMENTS IN AFRICA

cards.title: NATIONALISTS AND NATIONAL MOVMENTS IN AFRICA
body: Many Africans participated in the WW1st along side Britain and France hoping independence will be granted when the war ended but their hopes were betrayed.
Instead, former German colonies were awarded to Great Britain and colonial rule continued unchanged.
Africans became more active politically after the end of WWI. In many parts of Africa, movements emerged that demanded reform in the colonial system.
Although European colonial powers responded to such movements with force, they eventually began to make some reforms.

But the reforms introduced by the colonial powers did not satisfy many Africans Therefore, by the 1930s, a lot of Africans started to call for independence. These calls for independence came especially from a new generation of young African leaders. Most of these young leaders were educated abroad in Europe and the United States. Some of the most prominent new African leaders were Jomo Kenyatta of Kenya, Leopold Senghor of Senegal, Nnamdi Azikiwe of Nigeria.

The new African leaders were influenced by the ideas of Pan-Africanism. Pan-Africanism was an idea that proposed to unite all black Africans regardless of their national boundaries. Originally, it was popular in the United States and the Caribbean.

The two most prominent Pan- Africanists were W.E.B. Du Bois and Marcus Garvey. At the same time, an intellectual and cultural movement known as “Negritude” developed. Negritude sought to stress the uniqueness and importance of African culture and history.
Nationalism and National Movements in Asia A. Indian Movement for Independence
Mohandas Gandhi had become active in the Indian movement for self- rule before WWI. Because of his struggles, Indians had begun to call him India’s “Great Soul,” or Mahatma.
In protest, Gandhi organized numerous nonviolent protests and strikes against the British colonial system.

Gandhi was a believer in a nonviolent method of struggle. He protested British laws by using the methods of civil disobedience. Civil disobedience is a refusal to obey laws considered to be unjust and oppressive.

Gandhi based his ideas and methods of protest on the ancient Hindu idea of ahimsa, or reverence for life. He believed that the brutal British colonial rule could be defeated through love and non- violence. Gandhi called his non-violent acts of resistance, Satyagraha, a Sanskrit word for “truth and firmness.” The British response toward the opposition was harsh e.g. in 1919 the British army killed 400 peaceful protesters.

The invasion of Ethiopia by Italy under Mussolini
Also the military state of japan invaded Chinese territory of Manchuria in 1939 and invade invaded Beijing and Nanjing in 1936.
Dissatisfaction with the Versailles treaty ; both Germany and Italy didn’t accept the Versailles treaty that’s why
Hitler renounced the treaty and sent troops to the DMZ Rhine land in 1936 and increased army force and built air force the Luftwaffe.
Italy also wanted more lands and started colonial move in Africa.

The policy of appeasement : Britain and France didn’t responded to Hitler action they rather followed appeasement policy a belief that if Hitler got what he demands there could be peace( At Munich conference in 1938 Britain and France decided to give Hitler the Sudeten land of Czechoslovakia) and security which turned to the opposite.

Alliance system: Germany and Italy signed the Rome-berlin axis to help FRASISCO FRANCO in Spain in 1936 and later Germany signed the anti-comintern pact with japan .After invading Poland Germany signed the non-aggression pact with USSR in 1939.
